Making Earth Cool Again

André Corrêa do Lago and Túlio Andrade

Climate multilateralism is evolving into a two-tiered system in which high-level negotiations toward shared commitments and the real-world implementation of climate solutions become more mutually supportive. Only by unleashing such virtuous cycles can we keep the 1.5ºC target for global warming within reach.

SÃO PAULO—The recent confirmation by the United Nations Environment Programme that global temperatures are on track to exceed 1.5º Celsius above pre-industrial levels undoubtedly darkens the outlook for the coming years and decades. But fatalism is not an option. There is still an opportunity to make this “overshoot” temporary. By tying climate-change mitigation to people’s everyday concerns, and to countries’ development priorities, we can ensure that solutions reach the necessary scale before it is too late. The pace of implementation is already picking up since last year’s UN Climate Change Conference (COP30) in Belém, in the Brazilian Amazon. Inspired by the Indigenous concept of mutirão (meaning a communal mobilization or collective effort), the COP30 Presidency urged the international community to unite around three objectives: strengthening multilateralism, connecting that process to people’s everyday lives, and accelerating implementation of the Paris climate agreement.Through this mutirão, the COP30 Presidency sought to consolidate a process that had long been underway, unleashing climate strategies beyond the negotiation rooms and across different economic sectors and segments of society. Since the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) was opened for signatures at the 1992 Rio Earth Summit, three decades of diplomacy have created a structure that combines climate mitigation, adaptation, finance, technology sharing, capacity-building, and instruments for addressing loss and damage. By the end of 2024, the Paris agreement’s rulebook, initiated in 2016, was completed, establishing a cycle of periodic nationally determined contributions (decarbonization targets/plans) and global stocktaking (progress assessments).

But climate multilateralism has come to a crossroads. Even as ongoing negotiations remain necessary, the implementation gap for what has already been agreed remains abysmal. The challenge for each COP now is to deliver more than final communiqués. Each must also demonstrate how hard-won decisions, once implemented, will bring concrete improvements to peoples’ lives.During our own preparations for COP30, concerns about rising geopolitical tensions and socioeconomic challenges were aggravated by the news that the United States would withdraw once again from the Paris agreement. By the conference’s closing session, however, no other party had left the accord, and more than 50 decisions had been achieved by consensus. The collective commitment to fighting climate change was renewed: 194 countries recognized that the transition to low-carbon and climate-resilient development is not only desirable but unavoidable. Unlike the 1.5ºC overshoot, this kind of systemic change cannot be reversed.

The rise of a new development model confirms that climate multilateralism is working, even if the pace of progress remains frustrating. Under COP30’s Global Mutirão Decision, countries resolved to embark on a decade of climate-policy implementation, and signed on to a new Global Implementation Accelerator to keep 1.5°C within reach and trigger so-called “positive tipping points” (self-sustaining mitigation scenarios)—which may be our last chance to reverse the overshoot.At the same time, the COP30 Global Climate Action Agenda created a new “ecology” of solutions and those pioneering them, connecting previously fragmented efforts to make the broader implementation regime more efficient and resilient. The initiative was designed to engage non-state actors and organize the implementation of the Paris agreement’s first global stocktake, as agreed by consensus at COP28 in Dubai three years ago. The Belém Action Agenda was also structured around a “Granary of Solutions” comprising 120 action plans involving hundreds of stakeholders across 30 key objectives—from renewables, transportation, and cities to agriculture, forests, culture, and AI.Together, COP30’s global mobilization, negotiations, and Action Agenda revealed that the global climate regime is shifting from a negotiation track to a living system. Organically growing through the UNFCCC’s sophisticated institutional architecture, the COPs’ decision-making role among nation-states is now being complemented by a fast-growing implementation ecosystem.That means climate multilateralism itself is evolving into a two-tiered system in which negotiation and implementation become more mutually supportive. The first tier, anchored in consensus-based negotiations, retains its traditional function of creating rules, while the second tier operates at a faster, complementary pace, mobilizing coalitions of governments, subnational authorities, companies, civil-society organizations, financial institutions, and others to deliver on what has been adopted by consensus. The Tropical Forest Forever Facility and the Open Coalition on Compliance Carbon Markets, both launched at COP30, are examples of what this looks like in practice.On this second tier, the emphasis has been shifting toward rapid, large-scale mobilization of resources serving initiatives worldwide. As coalitions create demand, raise finance, share technologies, and build capacities, cooperation itself generates increasing returns. The more participants there are, the more attractive participation becomes to others. This implementation movement has allowed climate action to gain global scale, irrespective of backtracking by any specific country. As the net-zero transition connects economies, societies, and governments at all levels through sustainable development, implementation coalitions increasingly cut across ideological and geopolitical lines, including entrenched North-South negotiating divides. To translate agreed commitments into predictable and stable long-term planning, the COP30 Presidency proposed roadmaps to implement two of the most urgent, but challenging, policy programs: transitioning away from fossil fuels, and halting and reversing deforestation by 2030. Ongoing work will build on previous mandates toward mobilizing $1.3 trillion per year for developing countries.The benefits of climate multilateralism’s evolution into a two-tiered regime have only begun to be recognized. With the role of new participants in the implementation phase growing, the COP31 Presidency (shared by Turkey and Australia) is already pushing for an even stronger implementation track at this year’s conference in Antalya. Looking ahead, our collective ambition must be to elevate climate solutions from niche applications to the mainstream. By ensuring that the benefits reach everyone, everywhere, we can realize the promise of the climate-aligned development paradigm—a driver and precondition of competitiveness and of food, water, and energy security in the 21st century—and its potential to bring us back from the brink.
